home.heroLede: Operator-grade guides, private journeys, and a Cairo-based concierge — for travellers who want Egypt planned with care, not copied from a template.
home.standfirstLine1: Most travel sites treat Egypt as a checklist of monuments.
home.standfirstLine2: We treat it as a country with eighty million people, four major dialects, and several thousand years of opinions about itself.
home.standfirstAccent: The difference shows up in the details.

blog.footInSeasonBody:
October through March is the easier window for most of Egypt — clearer air, gentler light, and comfortable days for walking the sites.

High-season mornings book out first. Lock in the experiences that depend on light or limited permits before the rest of the trip falls into place.
blog.footPracticalBody:
Most first trips work best with a few unhurried days per region rather than a long checklist of cities.

When in doubt about timing, permits, or how to pair an experience with the rest of a day, ask us — that is what the concierge is for.

travelTips.footInSeasonBody:
October to April is the gentle window for a first trip — comfortable days, cool evenings, and the sites at their kindest.

Ramadan shifts each year; days run shorter and quieter, and some opening hours change. Worth planning around either way.
travelTips.footPracticalBody:
Most of these answers are the ones we'd give you on the phone — visas, money, dress, getting around.

If your question isn't here, ask us. The practical details are the easy part to get right with a little local knowledge.

nileCruises.footInSeasonBody:
November to March is peak on the river — dahabiyas and steamers are few and book months ahead. Reserve the small vessels early.

The water is lowest in November, rising through winter; sailing conditions improve into January.
nileCruises.footPracticalBody:
Choose the vessel before the itinerary — a dahabiya and a grand ship sail the same water and make two different trips.

Unsure which boat suits the trip? Ask us; matching the vessel to the traveller is the part that matters.

hieroglyphs.banner: Hieroglyphs can be read right-to-left, left-to-right, or top-to-bottom — direction depends on which way the bird and animal glyphs face.

hieroglyphs.cartoucheToggle: Wrap in a cartouche (the royal frame)
hieroglyphs.disclaimer: This is a phonetic transliteration — a fun, modern approximation. Ancient scribes used hieroglyphs symbolically and grammatically; names were typically written within a cartouche (oval frame) reserved for royalty. Letters such as C/K, E/I, F/V, and O/U/W share glyphs because ancient Egyptian didn't distinguish those sounds the way modern English does.

consent.headline: We use only essential cookies
consent.body: Travel2Egypt sets a small cookie to remember the language you are reading in. If you use our AI concierge, we also set a session cookie, t2e_session_id, so your conversation stays continuous across pages and visits — it lasts 30 days and is limited to travel2egypt.org. To protect the concierge from abuse, we process a one-way hashed version of your IP address and browser; the raw values are never stored or logged. We run no analytics, no advertising, and no visitor tracking.

tourSystem.grpDayCatEssay:
A small group is the middle path. You keep the structure of a guided day — the transfers, the tickets, a licensed Egyptologist who knows the site — but you share the cost and the company with a handful of other travellers rather than booking a car for your party alone.

Departures are fixed and the group is capped, so the day still moves at a human pace: no coach of forty, no waiting on stragglers. From six base cities — Cairo, Luxor, Aswan, Hurghada, Marsa Alam and Sharm El-Sheikh — the headline sites are within a day’s reach.

If you’d rather set your own hours, or travel with only your own party, the private day tours run the same routes one group at a time. Otherwise, choose your base city below and see which shared days depart from it.

pyramids.standfirstLead: Eight pyramids, a thousand years of trial and error. How to tell them apart at a glance —
pyramids.standfirstAccent: by their silhouettes, not their signage.

djoser.name: Djoser
djoser.desc: The first. Six stacked mastabas, designed by Imhotep — the moment Egypt began building skyward in stone.

meidum.name: Meidum
meidum.desc: A step pyramid skinned into a smooth one — that then sloughed its casing, leaving a lone tower in a ring of rubble.

bent.name: Bent
bent.desc: Begins at a steep 54°, loses its nerve halfway up and finishes at 43° — the geometry of a builder learning on the job.

red.name: Red
red.desc: Egypt's first true smooth-sided pyramid — broad, shallow, and named for the rosy limestone beneath its stripped casing.

khufu.name: Khufu
khufu.desc: The summit of the form. 146 metres at completion, and the only Wonder of the Ancient World still standing.

khafre.name: Khafre
khafre.desc: Shorter than Khufu, yet it looks taller — set on higher bedrock and still wearing a <gold>cap of original casing</gold>.

menkaure.name: Menkaure
menkaure.desc: The third Giza pyramid, a fraction of its neighbours — its <gold>lower courses sheathed in red Aswan granite</gold>.

hawara.name: Hawara
hawara.desc: A Middle Kingdom mound of mudbrick — once the gateway to the lost Labyrinth that Herodotus swore outdid the pyramids.

arabic.metaDescription: Forty Arabic words and phrases for travellers in Egypt — with the operator-grade cultural notes that matter.
arabic.standfirstAccent: Here are forty words that will make your trip warmer.
arabic.intro1: You don't need fluent Arabic to travel Egypt. English carries you through most hotels, museums, and tourist sites. But a few words used at the right moment shift how Egyptians respond to you — a market vendor smiles wider, a driver relaxes, a waiter remembers you. What follows is the small list that does the most work.
arabic.intro2: Egyptian Arabic differs from the formal Arabic taught in textbooks. The greetings, the rhythms, the cultural words — these are what you'll actually hear. We've written pronunciation as it sounds, not as it's spelled.

greetings.title: Greetings and warmth
greetings.operatorNote: As-salāmu ʿalaykum is universal and works in any context — Christian or Muslim, formal or casual. It's the safest opener you can use.

market.title: At a market or with a taxi
market.operatorNote: Bargaining is expected in markets and on souvenir prices — the first quote is almost always 2-3× what the vendor will accept. Counter at 30-40% and meet in the middle. Tone matters: friendly bargaining is a social ritual, aggressive bargaining is rude.

restaurant.title: At a restaurant
restaurant.operatorNote: Maʾalaysh deserves its own paragraph. It's the Egyptian word for accepting small inconveniences without escalation — spilled tea, late arrival, mild mishaps. Learning when to say it (and how to take it when said to you) is the cultural shortcut.

cultural.title: The cultural ones (used by everyone)
cultural.operatorNote: These five phrases are used by Egyptians of all backgrounds in essentially every conversation. Mā shāʾ Allāh in particular is important — if you compliment someone's child without saying it, you may make the parent uneasy.

arabic.warning: A few quick warnings. The word for "give me" (hāt) is technically valid Arabic but reads as rude to strangers — use mumkin (may I have…) instead. Pointing with one finger is impolite; gesture with the whole hand. And while in shāʾ Allāh is sincere from Egyptians, foreigners using it can sound dismissive — only say it if you genuinely mean "if circumstances allow," not as a non-answer.
arabic.closing: Egyptian Arabic carries warmth that English translation flattens. Even broken Arabic, attempted with goodwill, lands differently from good English. A market vendor who hears Lazīz! over a bite of koshari is being told something that "this is delicious" can't quite say. The forty words above are a starting point. The rest you learn by listening.
arabic.colophonNote: Field guide · pronunciation by ear, not by textbook · Egyptian dialect

egyptianGods.metaTitle: The Egyptian Gods, Mapped — Travel2Egypt Field Guide
egyptianGods.metaDescription: The Heliopolitan Ennead and the major deities orbiting it — a starting map for travellers who want to read temples, not just visit them.
egyptianGods.standfirstLead: A starting map of the gods,
egyptianGods.standfirstAccent: placed where you'll meet them on the ground.
egyptianGods.intro: Egyptian theology resists tidy genealogy. Different cities had different creator gods. Deities merged with each other over millennia. A "family tree" is, strictly, a fiction. What follows is the Heliopolitan Ennead — the most architecturally complete and most commonly encountered system — with the major secondary deities placed around it. It is the version you'll meet most often as you travel.
egyptianGods.closing: This is one tradition's map of the gods. Each city had its own. As you travel, you'll find some of these deities feel more present than others — Sobek dominates Kom Ombo, Horus rules Edfu, Khnum holds Elephantine. The map shifts with the geography.
egyptianGods.colophonNote: Phase 1 · six seeded deities · the rest to come. Solid lines run parent to child; dashed lines mark spouse pairs.

timeline.metaTitle: Three Thousand Years, In Order — Travel2Egypt Field Guide
timeline.metaDescription: Cleopatra is closer in time to the iPhone than to the Pyramids. A working chronology of pharaonic Egypt for travellers walking into the monuments.
timeline.standfirstLead: Cleopatra is closer in time to the iPhone than to the Pyramids.
timeline.standfirstAccent: Here's how three thousand years of pharaonic Egypt fits together.
timeline.figureCaption: Era widths drawn to scale — 1 unit ≈ 4 years. Tut omitted from the visual; he sits in the New Kingdom section below.
timeline.intro1: Most travellers arrive in Egypt with a sense that the pharaohs are a single thing — ancient, robed, monumental. Standing in Karnak or Giza, the temporal scale doesn't quite register: the Old Kingdom pyramid builders are as distant from the New Kingdom temple builders as we are from the Roman Empire. Ramses II ruled when Troy was being besieged. Cleopatra was born closer to our time than to the building of the Great Pyramid.
timeline.intro2: What follows is a working chronology — the periods, the key rulers, and what each era actually built — written so that when you walk into a monument, you know whose monument it is and where it sits in the larger story.

old.label: Old Kingdom · ~2686–2181 BC
old.frame: The Old Kingdom is the Pyramid Age — the period during which the stone pyramid was invented, perfected, and eventually outgrown. The capital was Memphis. The architecture is restrained and monumental; the surviving art has a frontal, symmetrical formality. This is the Egypt of dressed-stone certainty.
old.op: What travellers see of the Old Kingdom is pyramids and Saqqara. The temples and palaces are mostly gone; what survived are tombs, because they were built to survive. The frontal art style that feels "Egyptian" to modern eyes was perfected here.

inter1.label: First Intermediate Period · ~2181–2055 BC
inter1.frame: Civil war, decentralised power, regional rulers competing for legitimacy. No major monuments travellers visit; the era's interest is mostly archaeological. Worth knowing only because it explains why the Middle Kingdom afterward felt the need to perform reunification.

middle.label: Middle Kingdom · ~2055–1650 BC
middle.frame: The Middle Kingdom is the literary age — the period that produced Egypt's classical literature, refined administrative systems, and built more modestly than the Old Kingdom. The capital moved to Thebes and then to Itj-tawy. The pyramids returned but smaller, built of mud brick faced with stone.
middle.op: Middle Kingdom monuments are harder to find than Old or New Kingdom ones — many are eroded or lost. The Fayoum pyramid trip is the most accessible Middle Kingdom experience for most travellers.

inter2.label: Second Intermediate Period · ~1650–1550 BC
inter2.frame: Hyksos rule. The Asiatic Hyksos governed the Delta from Avaris; the rest of Egypt paid tribute or contested the territory. The Hyksos brought the chariot, the composite bow, and the horse to Egypt — innovations the New Kingdom would later turn into an empire.

new.label: New Kingdom · ~1550–1069 BC
new.frame: The New Kingdom is the empire era — Egypt at its most outward-looking, militarised, theatrical, and rich. The capital was Thebes (modern Luxor); the rulers built temple complexes on a scale never attempted before or since. This is the Egypt of the famous names — Hatshepsut, Akhenaten, Tutankhamun, Ramses II — and the period most travellers spend the most time in.
new.op: The New Kingdom is what most travellers come to Egypt to see. Karnak, Luxor Temple, the Valley of the Kings, Abu Simbel — all New Kingdom. If you have one week in Egypt, this is the era you spend most of it in.

inter3.label: Third Intermediate Period · ~1069–664 BC
inter3.frame: Decline and fragmentation. Libyan dynasties ruled the Delta; Nubian pharaohs (the 25th Dynasty) ruled the whole country from the south for a century. The era is undervalued — Nubian kings restored old temples and revived earlier artistic styles — but produced few headline monuments travellers visit on a standard itinerary.

late.label: Late Period · ~664–332 BC
late.frame: Persian conquests punctuated by brief Egyptian restorations. The Saite (26th) Dynasty revived archaic art deliberately, looking back to the Old Kingdom across two thousand years. Persians twice conquered Egypt; twice were thrown out. Some surviving Late Period temple work blends naturally into what travellers think of as "classical" Egyptian — the period is more present in standard sites than visitors realise.

ptolemaic.label: Ptolemaic Egypt · 332–30 BC
ptolemaic.frame: After Alexander the Great's conquest in 332 BC, Egypt was ruled by a Greek-Macedonian dynasty for three hundred years. The Ptolemies built in the Egyptian style but as Greeks ruling Egypt — temples that look pharaonic but were built when Rome was already rising. Most of the "classic" Egyptian temples travellers visit are actually Ptolemaic.
ptolemaic.op: Edfu Temple, Kom Ombo, Dendera, Philae — all Ptolemaic. These are the best-preserved temples in Egypt precisely because they're "newest." Travellers often assume they're New Kingdom or earlier; they're not.

roman.label: Roman Egypt and after · 30 BC onward
roman.frame: Rome inherited Egypt with Cleopatra's death. Some pharaonic traditions continued — late-Roman temple work at Philae, Kalabsha, Dendur — but pharaonic Egypt as a self-ruling civilisation ended in 30 BC. The timeline above stops there. Christianisation, the Arab conquest of 641 AD, the Mamluks, the Ottomans, modern Egypt: each is a long story of its own, beyond the chronology this guide covers.

djoser.name: Djoser
djoser.body: Commissioned the Step Pyramid at Saqqara — the world's first large stone building. Designed by Imhotep, the architect who became Egypt's first individual named in history.

sneferu.name: Sneferu
sneferu.body: Built three pyramids — Meidum, Bent, and Red — figuring out through experimentation how to make a true pyramid stand. The father of Khufu and the unsung hero of Egyptian engineering.

khufu.name: Khufu
khufu.body: Built the Great Pyramid at Giza — the largest stone building ever made in antiquity, and the only Wonder of the Ancient World still standing. Almost nothing else about his reign survives.

khafre.name: Khafre
khafre.body: Built the second Giza pyramid — slightly shorter than Khufu's but on higher bedrock, so it looks taller. Almost certainly commissioned the Sphinx.

menkaure.name: Menkaure
menkaure.body: The third and smallest Giza pyramid. Sheathed in red Aswan granite at its base — the lower courses are still visible. The compression of the form after Khufu and Khafre marks the end of the Pyramid Age proper.

mentuhotep.name: Mentuhotep II
mentuhotep.body: Reunified Egypt after the First Intermediate Period and founded the Middle Kingdom. His mortuary temple at Deir el-Bahari predates Hatshepsut's — when you visit her three-terraced temple, you're standing next to his, partly demolished but still visible.

senusret3.name: Senusret III
senusret3.body: A strong administrator who expanded Egypt's reach into Nubia. His surviving statues are striking for their realistic, careworn faces — a sharp break from the idealised faces of earlier kings.

amenemhat3.name: Amenemhat III
amenemhat3.body: Built the Hawara pyramid and the famous Labyrinth complex beside it — once one of the wonders of the ancient world, now almost entirely gone. Developed the Fayoum oasis as agricultural land.

hatshepsut.name: Hatshepsut
hatshepsut.body: One of Egypt's few female pharaohs and one of the most successful. Her mortuary temple at Deir el-Bahari rises in three terraces against the cliff face — the most architecturally distinctive royal monument in Egypt.

thutmose3.name: Thutmose III
thutmose3.body: Hatshepsut's stepson and eventual successor. Expanded the empire to its largest extent in seventeen military campaigns. After Hatshepsut's death he attempted to erase her name from monuments — partly successfully, partly not.

akhenaten.name: Akhenaten
akhenaten.body: Religious revolutionary. Tried to replace traditional polytheism with worship of a single sun disk (Aten); moved the capital to Amarna and reigned from there. His successors dismantled his city, smashed his statues, and tried to erase him from the record. The art of his reign — naturalistic, elongated, unlike anything before or since — survives.

tut.name: Tutankhamun
tut.body: A minor king famous only because his tomb survived intact — the one royal tomb in the Valley of the Kings that escaped looting in antiquity. His treasure now anchors the Grand Egyptian Museum at Giza, the only place in the world where the entire find is shown together.

ramses.name: Ramses II
ramses.body: Reigned 66 years. Egypt's great builder: Abu Simbel cut into the cliff at the southern frontier, the Ramesseum on the Theban west bank, vast additions to Karnak and Luxor, his face carved on statues everywhere from the Delta to Nubia. Most ancient pharaohs you've heard of are him.

ptolemy1.name: Ptolemy I
ptolemy1.body: Alexander the Great's Macedonian general. After Alexander's death he took Egypt as his share of the empire and founded a Greek dynasty that ruled the country in pharaonic guise for three hundred years. He also founded the Library of Alexandria.

cleopatra.name: Cleopatra VII
cleopatra.body: The last pharaoh of Egypt. Macedonian Greek by ancestry; spoke Egyptian, unusually for her dynasty. Her alliance and rivalry with Rome ended with her suicide in 30 BC. With her death, pharaonic Egypt ends.

timeline.closing: Three thousand years is hard to hold in your head. The point of the chronology above isn't to memorise it — it's to give you a rough map. When you walk into a temple, ask first: which era was this built? Once you can answer that, the temple tells its story. The columns make sense. The reliefs make sense. The scale makes sense. Knowing whose monument it is — and where they sit in the larger sequence — is the difference between sightseeing and reading the country.
timeline.colophonNote: Field guide · dates approximate · chronology after Shaw, Oxford History of Ancient Egypt
